discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable absorber) for femtosecond solid-state lasers
motivation: Nearly every ultrafast laboratory in the world rests on three contributions. Peter Moulton invented the titanium-doped sapphire laser (1982-86), a gain medium broad enough to support femtosecond pulses and tunable across the near infrared. Wilson Sibbett's group discovered self-mode-locking of Ti:sapphire (1991), explained as Kerr-lens mode-locking, which gave simple, robust sub-10-femtosecond oscillators. Ursula Keller invented the semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM, 1992), which made passive mode-locking reliable across solid-state and later semiconductor and fibre lasers. Together they turned femtosecond pulses from a dye-laser specialty into a turnkey tool. These oscillators seed chirped-pulse amplifiers, drive attosecond science and frequency combs, and are used in multiphoton microscopy, ophthalmic surgery and precision micromachining. This enabling work has transformed physics, chemistry, biology and medicine, and it deserves recognition while its pioneers are with us.
